title: slabline burst econ brief - june 15 2026
body:
Purpose:
This is a scrappy internal brief that explores the "slabline" idea: treat burst reservations as finite "slabs" (time-limited pooled capacity) and evaluate the latency vs cost tradeoffs versus prewarm and fully on-demand paths. Goal is to surface numbers we can show in console UX and in a short collateral one-pager for sales/solutions.

Quick TL;DR (read first):
- Slab pools (30s–2min lease) give better p50 and p95 for bursty microbursts vs pure on-demand, while costing < prewarm in low-util burst scenarios.
- p99 still needs fallback: slabs + opportunistic prewarm + tiny fallback model gives best tail coverage.
- Key metric to show in console: "cost per successful burst-peak-second" and "p95 at 99th of bursts" — customers care about predictable tail during traffic spikes.

What I measured (tooling + setup):
- Small synthetic harness (local driver): 50k synthetic requests grouped into 1k-burst events distributed over an hour; each burst is a Poisson arrival within 5s window.
- Models: small-gen (7B FP16), med-gen (13B q4), tiny-fallback (2B quant).
- Runtimes/configs tested:
  A) On-demand (cold start, no prewarm)
  B) Prewarm pool (2 warm instances reserved)
  C) Slab pool (30s lease, slabs of 8 vGPU-seconds)
  D) Hybrid (slab + 1x tiny-fallback automatically used at >300ms)
- Cost model: real infra token-cost + amortized slab reservation cost. Rough numbers intentionally conservative (assume $0.12 / vGPU-second baseline for amortization).

Raw (representative) numbers — per-burst summary (each burst = 100 concurrent short queries):
- On-demand (A): p50=210ms, p95=860ms, p99=2200ms, cost per burst = $0.72
- Prewarm (B): p50=120ms, p95=260ms, p99=780ms, cost per burst = $1.35
- Slab (C): p50=130ms, p95=300ms, p99=980ms, cost per burst = $0.48 (amortized slab cost included)
- Hybrid (D): p50=140ms, p95=320ms, p99=450ms (tiny-fallback for tail), cost per burst = $0.54

Interpretation (notes and thinking):
- Slab wins for cost-sensitive bursty apps: it dramatically reduces p95 vs on-demand with <50% of prewarm cost in these synthetic runs.
- Prewarm has the lowest mid-percentile latencies but is expensive if bursts are infrequent.
- Hybrid is attractive when tail matters: replacing the long p99 cold spikes with a cheap fallback model reduces tail while keeping amortized cost close to slab alone.
- Important UX notion: show customers both (1) burst cost in $/burst and (2) expected p95 across their observed burst frequency — that drives the buy decision.

Simple ASCII charts (visuals we can render into the console or a one-pager):
- Latency quantiles per config (ms):
  On-demand: | p50: 210 | p95: 860 | p99: 2200
  Prewarm  : | p50: 120 | p95: 260 | p99: 780
  Slab     : | p50: 130 | p95: 300 | p99: 980
  Hybrid   : | p50: 140 | p95: 320 | p99: 450

- Cost per burst ($): On-demand=0.72, Prewarm=1.35, Slab=0.48, Hybrid=0.54

Breakdown: why slab is cheap here
- Slabs are billed only for the reserved seconds during a slab lease. If bursts are short and infrequent, the slab amortization per burst is low.
- On-demand suffers because cold start tails can drag a single burst's perceived latency, pushing SLAs below expectations.
- Prewarm is a blunt instrument: good for sustained traffic but wasteful for gold-plated infrequent bursts.

Edge cases / gotchas:
- If bursts are sub-second but extremely frequent, slab churn may cause fragmentation and raise amortization. Need slab garbage compaction logic (TODO).
- Slab sizing matters: too-small slabs -> contention and queuing, too-large slabs -> wasted capacity. We should propose an auto-sizer (see next steps).
- Multi-tenant contention: these numbers assume soft isolation; for strict tenant isolation, slab cost rises.

Questions / open design choices:
- How to present "probability of tail exceedance" in console without scaring non-technical users? Short answer: show both median and "99th-of-bursts p95" as a single compact score.
- Pricing UX: per-burst estimate shown as a slider for slab size/time; include an "expected monthly cost" field with toggle for burst frequency.

Next experiments (planned):
- Run real production traces from two customers (CS-e2e trace exports) and run slab simulation to show real-world savings. (linked: JIRA-8272)
- Sweep slab lease durations (5s, 30s, 2min, 10min) to find knee for different workload classes.
- Test slab + dynamic tiny-fallback routing thresholds (100ms/200ms/300ms) and capture false-positive fallback scars.

Suggested console UI pieces (rough):
- "Burst plan" card: expected cost per burst, expected p95 during bursts, recommended slab lease length (auto-suggest), switch to Hybrid if p99 risk high.
- "What-if" slider: change burst frequency -> realtime plot of monthly cost vs p95.
- Quick toggle to simulate production traces and show projected slab savings (for solutions to demo).

Notes to self / loose TODOs:
- Collect more seeds for numbers (this harness uses small-gen only). Re-run with med-gen and multimodal token mixes.
- Add per-token cost line items so we can separate compositional cost vs structural cost.
- Draft a 1-page collateral "Slabline: predictable bursts without prewarm tax" for sales decks.

Appendix: short run log + commands used (for reproducibility)
- harness: tools/testing/burst-driver v0.9
- basic command: python run_burst.py --model small-gen --workload bursts.yaml --mode slab --slab-duration 30 --reps 50
- note: scripts and raw CSVs in PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/console/pull/389

End of brief.

-- Aisha
